title: Leaving and moving after fallout
summary: Stay in unless an immediate danger such as a fire, gas leak, collapse or serious injury forces you out, or officials tell you to leave. If you must go, cover your mouth, nose and skin, move away from the explosion and the heaviest fallout to the nearest good shelter, and take off your outer clothes and wash when you get there.
doFirst: Leave only if an immediate danger such as a fire, gas leak, building collapse or serious injury forces you out, or officials tell you to (Ready.gov).

Have to go? Cover your mouth and nose with a mask, cloth or towel (CDC), and if it doesn’t slow you down, wear a hat, gloves and an outer layer you can take off (this app’s own caution; fallout lands on clothing and bare skin, FEMA planning guidance).
Go to the nearest building that gives good shelter, moving away from the explosion and from where the fallout is heaviest (CDC, FEMA planning guidance).

When you get there, take off your outer clothes and shoes before you go in or just inside the door, away from others, and wash (CDC, FEMA planning guidance; Radiation decontamination). See Coming in from outside.
Told to evacuate? Listen for the routes, shelters and procedures officials give, and follow them (Ready.gov).

blocks.p: Leave only if an immediate danger such as a fire, gas leak, building collapse or serious injury forces you out, or officials tell you to (Ready.gov). How long to stay in otherwise is in How long to stay in.

list: FEMA’s planning guidance: stay inside unless threatened by fire, building collapse, medical needs or another immediate threat. Fast-spreading fires may call for leaving at once.
FEMA’s 72-hour guidance: don’t leave unless officials give other instructions or your shelter is threatened by fire or collapse.
CDC: unless you have a life-threatening situation, don’t leave your building or shelter until emergency officials say you can.

blocks.p: A CO alarm still means what Carbon monoxide says, even during a fallout warning: “CO alarm sounding? Don’t look for the cause. Get everyone outside into fresh air now” (CPSC).
Cold is handled inside first, by the rules in Living in a closed-up house. A shelter that is poor can be swapped once for a much better one nearby, by the times in Where to shelter from fallout.

blocks.label: Carbon monoxide and burning fuel indoors

list: FEMA strongly discourages people leaving on their own because of the risks (FEMA planning guidance).
Unless a fire or other immediate danger forces you, no evacuation should be tried until there is basic information about where the fallout fell (FEMA planning guidance).

FEMA plans to move first the people whose lives are in immediate danger. People who are not hurt and have adequate shelter and food and water are a low priority for early evacuation (FEMA planning guidance).
Outside you may meet fires, downed power lines and broken gas lines. Driving may be very dangerous or impossible because of crashed cars and rubble on the roads (NYC Health).
Ready.gov counts serious injury among the immediate dangers that can force you out, and FEMA’s planning guidance names medical needs and medical emergencies.
If you are sick or injured, listen for instructions on how and where to get medical care (Ready.gov).
First aid is in Emergency.

blocks.p: This app’s caution, not a source’s: with no word from officials, nobody can tell you whether a hospital is open or can be reached. Before anyone carries a casualty out through fallout, be as sure as you can where you are going and that you can get there.

list: If officials give a route, use it (Ready.gov, NYC Health): routes are chosen to keep your radiation exposure as low as possible (NYC Health).

With no route given: move away from the explosion and from the areas with the most fallout (FEMA planning guidance), and at right angles to the fallout’s path if you know it (FEMA planning guidance). Officials may know the path; you may not.

Fallout can make radiation dangerous downwind of the explosion (FEMA planning guidance). But the wind high up can carry it in a different direction from the wind you feel, and in more than one direction (FEMA planning guidance).
Fallout is often visible as it falls, about the size of fine sand or table salt (FEMA planning guidance).
In a town, connections between buildings and tunnels can keep you under cover for part of the way (FEMA planning guidance).
A car is not a shelter (FEMA planning guidance). Don’t shelter in it (NYC Health): get into a building.
If you must leave and have a car, fallout on the car is not a reason not to use it (FEMA planning guidance).
Expect blocked roads: rubble and disabled vehicles can make driving difficult or impossible (FEMA planning guidance, NYC Health).
Cover your mouth and nose with a mask, cloth or towel (CDC). No mask? Use a handkerchief or clothing (NYC Health). Don’t wait for a mask: you don’t need one to evacuate (NYC Health).
Fallout lands on clothing and bare skin, such as the head and hands (FEMA planning guidance). It catches easily in shirt collars and around the tops of shoes (FEMA 72-hour guidance).
Try not to touch your eyes, nose and mouth (Ready.gov).

sections.h: Clean off on the way and when you arrive

list: Leaving a fallout area or going into a shelter: brush off, take off or change your outer clothes and shoes, and wipe off bare skin (FEMA planning guidance).
On the move, FEMA’s 72-hour guidance is quick, dry cleaning, such as changing or shaking off the outer layer.
When you get in, wash as in Coming in from outside.
Taking in someone who was outside can save their life without putting your own at risk (CDC).

Arriving: take off your outer layer of clothes and shoes before you go in, or just inside the door, away from others (CDC; Radiation decontamination). Once inside, wash the parts of your body that were uncovered, then put on clean clothes if you can (CDC).
Letting someone in: ask them to do the same (CDC).
Bring pets with you (NYC Health); the federal government advises against leaving them behind (FEMA planning guidance). Wash them when you arrive, as in Coming in from outside.
If you have evacuated, don’t go back until local authorities tell you to (Ready.gov).
Whether and when you can go home depends on where it is, and is very hard to predict (NYC Health).
